_spec.law: Facts resolve to the original verified claim record. A layout rebuild does not reverify reporting.

dek.text: Dallas cameras on sanitation trucks photographed more than {{number:c14}} code concerns in four months. The Dallas Morning News reported {{number:c15}} citations.

introduction.text: [Dallas began using {{number:c30}} AI-powered cameras on bulky sanitation trucks in mid-April](c30). [The cameras face sideways and capture images from the public right of way](c5). [Software looks for property conditions such as bulk trash, tires, illegal dumping and graffiti](c8).

[In four months the cameras photographed more than {{number:c14}} code concerns, the Dallas Morning News reported](c14). [That resulted in {{number:c15}} citations at {{number:c15:1}} properties, primarily in southern Dallas](c15). A flagged image is a concern, not a violation, and the steps between the two decide who gets a visit.

sections.heading: How a flag becomes a visit

paragraphs.text: [The process the paper described starts with a still image taken along a truck's route](c20). [Software flags a potential concern](c21) [and a code compliance analyst reviews it](c22). [City workers then choose between taking no action, sending a courtesy notice and opening a case](c23). [A code officer inspects the property in person](c24), [and a citation can be issued only after an actual violation is confirmed](c25).

[The city's briefing to its Finance Committee said the system is neither a staff replacement nor automated ticketing](c12) [and that a person stays in the loop](c13). [It said faces and license plates are blurred](c6). [City Detect's chief executive later told a council committee that the company had expanded its blurring to cover a person's full image](c39).

[A Dallas Morning News analysis of city data placed about {{number:c17}} of the {{number:c17:1}} images in southern Dallas](c17). [Properties in east and southeast Oak Cliff drew the most citations, with {{number:c16}}](c16).

[Council member Chad West, who represents Oak Cliff, questioned whether the technology could unintentionally target southern Dallas residents who face citations for conditions they can't afford to repair](c26). [Code Compliance Director Chris Christian said the cameras run along existing sanitation routes across the city and are not meant to target communities by income or demographics](c40).

sections.heading: What changed and what is still unmeasured

paragraphs.text: [The city sent about {{number:c19}} courtesy notices between June and August, and a courtesy notice is not a citation or a fine](c19). [The city says a courtesy notice opens no enforcement case and sets no formal deadline](c35). [Courtesy notices will carry a QR code to the city's Housing and Community Empowerment resource page](c44), [and the code department plans to soften their wording](c34).

[Figures reported in October count {{number:c31}} observations reviewed, {{number:c31:1}} courtesy notices sent and {{number:c31:2}} field inspections](c31). [Those figures measure different parts of the program and are not a step by step count of cases from detection to enforcement](c33).

[The contract costs {{money:c10}} a year](c10), [subject to annual City Council appropriations](c9), [and the city may end it on {{number:c11}} days' written notice](c11). [In September the paper reported that Dallas had not completed a comprehensive evaluation or a return on investment analysis](c29). [Staff told the committee they plan to improve detection accuracy, connect the system to city databases, develop performance measures and report on safeguards and outcomes](c41). [The city gave no timeline for those steps](c42).
